Czech oil players to replace remaining Russian volumes in state reserves  50% of Czech stocks are Russian crude  CPC Kazakhstan blend selected for storage  Stocks support Litvinov, Kralupy plants Czech oil refinery, transportation and state storage companies are working together to replace the remaining Russian oil held in the country’s strategic stockpiles – which amounts to around half – a spokesperson for its state reserves authority told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, on Nov. 9. On Nov. 6, Czech oil refiner Orlen Unipetrol, state-owned oil pipeline company Mero, and the State Authority for Management of Strategic Reserves signed a cooperation agreement paving the way for a phase-out of Russian crude from the country’s reserves. “We currently have around half [Russian] oil in reserves for Unipetrol’s refineries,” Jakub Linka, an SSHR spokesman, said in a telephone interview, with the remainder “a Norwegian oil mix [including] Johan Sverdrup for the Litvinov refinery, and an Azeri mix for the Kralupy refinery.” He added: “The memorandum is a first step in replacing the remaining Russian oil which amounts to half, 45 days out of the European Union’s obligatory 90-day oil reserve.” Linka said a further agreement still needs to be signed by the three parties setting out the specific timelines and other details of the oil reserves switch. Orlen Unipetrol has selected a CPC Kazakhstan-type oil blend as its preferred crude to be kept in the state reserves for possible emergency use, as it can be used by both Czech refineries. The larger Litvinov refinery is capable of processing oil with a higher sulfur content, while Kralupy uses a lower sulfur mix. The three Czech oil players still have to determine how suitable the CPC blend is for long term storage, Linka added. “The evaluation could take a year or more, this will be covered by the final agreements,” he said. The Czech Republic switched its oil supply to exclude Russian flows in March 2025 – amid a broad European shift away from Russian hydrocarbons following the Ukraine war – and now gets crude via the Trans-Alpine Pipeline, beginning at the Italian port of Trieste. The European country was previously largely reliant on Russian oil transported by the huge Druzhba pipeline system. The Litvinov refinery has an annual capacity to process 5.8 million metric tons of oil, while Kralupy is smaller at 3.3 million mt/year. — Chris Johnstone Iraq in talks with OPEC to raises its production, export ceiling: INA  Iraq's OPEC production quota at 4.431 mil b/d  Minister cites five decades of challenges  Current production sits at 3.9 million b/d Iraq is in talks with OPEC to increase its oil production and set a higher export ceiling, the state-run Iraqi News Agency reported Nov. 7, citing oil minister Bassem Khudair. “Iraq deserves an increase in production rates to generate the financial revenues necessary for developing infrastructure and implementing government plans,” the minister said, according to the INA statement. “Dialogue is under way with OPEC to raise the export ceiling, in view of Iraq's particular circumstances and the nature of the challenges it has faced over the past five decades.” OPEC has yet to respond to a request for comment on the matter Nov. 9. Iraq’s production quota under the OPEC+ agreement is 4.431 million barrels/day. Output was 3.9 million b/d in September, according to the latest Platts OPEC+ survey by S&P Global Energy. — Claudia Carpenter Operations at Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline unaffected by fresh attack: SPA  Pipeline sustains attack, fire extinguished  Saudi loads 2.8 mil b/d at Yanbu in October  Capacity expansion planned beyond 7 mil b/d Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, a key conduit linking eastern fields with the western port of Yanbu, came under attack again on Nov. 9, although there was no impact on operations, state news reported. In a statement, the Saudi Press Agency quoted an official source at the Saudi energy ministry as saying the 7 million barrel/ day pipeline was “targeted” in the Medina region, “resulting in a limited fire that was extinguished by emergency response teams.” No injuries or fatalities were reported, the official said, adding that “emergency response teams and specialized technical teams responded immediately following the attack and took the necessary measures to secure the site and ensure its safety.” It did not speculate on who was responsible for the attack. Representatives for Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Platts Nov. 9. The 1,200 km pipeline — which is connected to the huge crude processing facility in Abqaiq — represents an alternative export route for Saudi crude flows in the event of disruptions through the pivotal Strait of Hormuz, which hosted 20 million b/d of crude and products prior to the US-Iran war in February. After war broke out, the kingdom quickly rerouted flows through the East-West Piepline, but it came under attack by drones in early September, Riyadh said, resulting in a days-long shutdown. By Oct. 6, the pipeline was back pumping 5.8 million b/d, according to state media. In an earnings call on Nov. 3, meanwhile, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser told analysts that the pipeline is undergoing preliminary engineering work for a “major” expansion to take capacity to “much more” than its existing 7 million b/d. ©2026 S&P Global Inc. reports.ftext: www.spglobal.com/energy Platts Oilgram News Volume 104 / Issue 221 / November 10, 2026 Inside this issue Shell urges conventional jet investment as fuel security concerns sharpen  Conventional jet to remain aviation’s main fuel for decades: Shell  Middle East jet/kerosene output forecast below 815,000 b/d in Q4: CERA  Airlines urge investment in independent supply routes Aviation must keep investing in conventional jet fuel supply chains alongside sustainable aviation fuel, as Middle East disruptions expose weaknesses in infrastructure and supply arrangements, a Shell Aviation executive said Nov. 10 at the IATA Aviation Energy Forum in Guangzhou. Conventional jet will remain central to aviation for decades, requiring investment in alternative supplies, trading capabilities and storage to strengthen energy security, Doris Tan, head of Shell Aviation Asia-Pacific and Middle East, said at a panel. “Conventional jet is the main fuel that will be needed in aviation for many decades to come,” Tan said. “We need to really invest in supply contingency and the infrastructure projects.” Middle Eastern jet/kerosene production is projected to remain below 815,000 barrels/day in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.05 million b/d a year earlier, according to S&P Global Energy CERA's November aviation outlook. Refined product exports through the Strait of Hormuz are expected to remain low through year-end and potentially into the first half of 2027. The disruption is also feeding into Asian jet fuel economics with Singapore jet/kerosene-Dubai cracks strengthening $10.4/b to $66.2/b in October, according to CERA. OPEC production jumped 2.6 million b/d to 23.84 million b/d, with Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait accounting for the bulk of this increase. The additional production is expected to translate into about one cargo of crude oil shipped from Algeria to Indonesia each month, Pertamina Deputy President Director Oki Muraza said in a discussion Nov. 9. “Given the current global situation, with disruptions to one-fifth of the world's oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, we are stepping up efforts to bring barrels home. For example, we have just secured an acquisition in Algeria, which is expected to add around 32,000 b/d of oil production. In theory, this would translate into one cargo arriving from Algeria in Indonesia each month,” Muraza said. The acquisition is part of Pertamina's efforts to secure oil supplies from regions outside conflict-affected areas, particularly the Middle East, he said. Pertamina, through its affiliate PT Pertamina Algeria Eksplorasi Produksi (PAEP), agreed to acquire Spanish energy company Moeve's interests in three onshore oil fields in Algeria's Berkine Basin. The deal covers Moeve's stakes in the Rhourde el Khrouf, Bir el Msana and Ourhoud fields. Completion remains subject to customary conditions, including approval from Algerian authorities. Neither company disclosed the transaction value, the companies said in separate statements Nov. 4. Pertamina said Nov. 4 that the acquisition was part of its “Bring the Barrel Home” initiative, which aims to optimize production from overseas upstream assets to support oil and gas supplies to Indonesia. In December 2025, Pertamina shipped its first 1-million-barrel crude cargo from Algeria after extending the production-sharing contract for Block 405A, securing its operations in the country for another 25 years. The cargo departed from Port Arzew in Oran. In June 2026, a tanker carrying about 450,000 barrels of Algerian crude was scheduled to arrive at Pertamina's Cilacap refinery in Central Java to support refinery operations and domestic fuel supplies. Outside Algeria, Pertamina also holds upstream interests in Iraq and Malaysia, with part of its international portfolio managed through its 71.09% stake in France-listed Maurel & Prom. Expansion The company is looking to expand the overseas portfolio further through acquisitions of oil and gas assets in North Africa and South America, as it seeks to diversify its crude supplies away from regions exposed to geopolitical conflicts, Muraza said. “We are targeting mergers and acquisitions for oil and gas fields in North Africa, where there is no war, as well as in Latin America or South America,” he said. The company was also finalizing an expansion into Latin America through its subsidiary Maurel & Prom, Muraza said. “We are also finalizing our move into Latin America through our subsidiary, M&P. As we continue to increase national production capacity in line with the government's target of reaching 1 million b/d by 2030, we need to secure supplies ahead of 2030,” Muraza said, adding that Pertamina currently accounts for 69% of Indonesia's national oil production. “We are pursuing significant inorganic expansion through mergers and acquisitions, acquiring and buying oil and gas fields. We have successfully done this in North Africa, and we are now working on opportunities in South America,” he said. Deputy Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Yuliot Tanjung, during a meeting with the Regional Representatives Council (DPD) Nov. 9, broadcast on YouTube, said Indonesia was targeting oil production of 900,000-1 million b/d by 2029. reports.ftext: Volume 104 / Issue 216 / November 10, 2026 (continued on page 19) Market analysis International Crude OPEC+ output rebounds in Oct, as Middle East export recovery continues: Platts survey  Production up 2.82 mil b/d on month  Output hits wartime high  Group still producing well below quota OPEC+ crude output rose by 2.82 million barrels/day month over month to hit a US-Iran wartime high in October, as exports from the Middle East continued to rebound, the latest Platts OPEC+ survey from S&P Global Energy found. OPEC+ produced 38.09 mil b/d in October, still well below output of 42.89 million b/d in February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran. The decline from February is also partially due to the UAE leaving OPEC in May. OPEC production jumped 2.6 million b/d to 23.84 million b/d, with Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait accounting for the bulk of this increase. Middle East producers in the group are recovering production after attacks on energy infrastructure and severe shipping restrictions linked to the conflict in the region caused production to collapse earlier in 2026. Non-OPEC participants in the OPEC+ agreement increased production by 220,000 b/d to 14.25 million b/d in October. This was led by Russia, which benefited from a two-week break in Ukrainian attacks on its refinery network in the second half of the month. OPEC+ is grappling with volatile oil prices. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed Dated Brent at $118.76/b on Oct. 30 — down almost $10/b compared with the start of the month. Prices have since fallen further, with Dated Brent assessed at $91.76/b (continued on page 3) OIL FUTURES: Crude dips after Trump says new strikes on Iran ‘highly unlikely’  Diplomatic efforts fuel de-escalation hopes  Persian Gulf exports drop below 5 million b/d in Oct  Bahri Oil sends four ships via Hormuz on Nov. 10 Crude oil futures settled lower Nov. 10 amid growing expectations of a de-escalation between the US and Iran after US President Donald Trump downplayed the chances of military strikes. NYMEX December WTI settled 81 cents/barrel lower at $86.04/b, and ICE January Brent declined $1.08/b to $91.49/b. “The market has continued to unwind some of the geopolitical risk premium built into prices in recent weeks as expectations grow that the conflict between the US and Iran could move towards de-escalation,” Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a note by ING Nov. 10. Trump, speaking to reporters on Nov. 9, said that more US strikes against Iran were “highly unlikely” and that there is “positive momentum” behind efforts to end the conflict. “Crude oil prices dipped as hopes build that recent diplomatic efforts [would lead] to an end of the Middle East conflict. [US President Donald] Trump said it is highly unlikely he would order extensive strikes on Iran while there are peace negotiations going on,” ANZ Research analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes wrote in a note Nov. 10. NYMEX December RBOB settled 4.21 cents/gallon lower at $2.6088/gal, and December ULSD declined 8.39 cents/gal to $4.1309/gal. The physical Brent/Futures spread fell to a $2.12/barrel discount on Nov. 9, according to data from Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, while an unusual number of North Sea cargoes have been left unsold. Before early July, physical Brent had not traded at such a steep discount to futures since 2022 at the height of the coronavirus pandemic. It also reflects a collapse since early October, when the Brent/ Futures spread was in strong backwardation at over $30/b. A similar effect was occurring in the Brent prompt structure, with the one-week-ahead Brent CFD crashing by about $32/b since Oct. 7, putting it almost in contango. That reflects weakening prompt Dated Brent versus forward Brent, and therefore a well-supplied market. In the week ended Nov. 9, the Dated Brent differential — the most competitive among Brent, Forties, Oseberg, Ekofisk, Troll and WTI Midland — sank to its lowest level since 2020. These spreads have been highly volatile since the start of the US-Iran war in late February, which has roiled crude markets by disrupting flows through the Strait of Hormuz, boosting prices and slashing global inventories, and prompting regular spasms in the futures market on expectations of either peace talks or further escalation. However, the recent erosion in prompt demand for Dated Brent has been driven mainly by high freight rates, which have constrained the eastward flow of North Sea crudes and WTI Midland. At the same time, competitively priced Middle Eastern barrels — now coming out of the Persian Gulf at greater levels, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea data — have stifled arbitrage opportunities for North Sea and US crude to clear into Asia. With reduced Asian demand for WTI Midland crude in recent weeks, more US oil is making its way to Europe, adding to an already well-supplied Northwest European crude market, although traders note that the US can absorb excess barrels. And an equally well-supplied Mediterranean crude market — flush with cheap CPC Blend from Kazakhstan — is not serving as an outlet for barrels from the Americas, but is rather pushing transatlantic volumes toward the North Sea. Unsold cargoes These factors have led North Sea barrels to go without buyers. Platts data shows 31 offers for crudes within the Dated Brent basket left outstanding at the London close across 10 sessions between Oct. 27 and Nov. 9. All rights reserved. 3 Indonesia offers 4 oil, gas blocks to expand production amid energy security drive  Blocks span more than 33,900 sq km for exploration  Indonesia applies 2 production-sharing mechanisms Indonesia has offered four oil and gas blocks spanning more than 33,900 square kilometers to investors for exploration, as it seeks to attract upstream capital, expand reserves and boost future domestic production to ensure energy security, the Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry said in a statement Nov. 10. “To increase investment while maintaining national energy availability in the future, the energy ministry continues to offer working areas to encourage oil and gas exploration and development, which are expected to increase national production and add new reserves,” the statement from the ministry quoted Director General of Oil and Gas Laode Sulaeman as saying. The four blocks are Cerera offshore Papua, Areca-Bruni onshore and offshore Southwest Papua, South Tanimbar offshore in the Arafura Sea, and Namori offshore East Nusa Tenggara, the ministry said. The offering provides new exploration opportunities for upstream companies, with the government allowing investors to choose between cost recovery and gross split production-sharing contracts, it said. Indonesia uses two production-sharing mechanisms in its oil and gas sector — cost recovery and gross split. Under the cost recovery scheme, contractors can recover eligible operating costs from production before the remaining output is shared with the government. Under the gross split scheme, production is divided based on an agreed share, but contractors must cover their own operating costs. Namori, located offshore East Nusa Tenggara, has estimated resources of 17.475 billion barrels of oil or 38.5 trillion cubic feet of gas, while South Tanimbar in the Arafura Sea is estimated to hold 5.6 Tcf of gas. Cerera in offshore Papua has estimated resources of 1.487 billion barrels of oil and 1.3 Tcf of gas. The block previously received a participation submission, but the documents were deemed incomplete under the applicable regulations and were not evaluated. The prospective bidder remains eligible to participate in a subsequent direct offer, the ministry said. Meanwhile, Areca-Bruni, covering onshore and offshore Southwest Papua, is estimated to contain 2.985 billion barrels of oil equivalent, the statement said. Minimum firm commitments Minimum firm commitments for the first three years include geological and geophysical studies, as well as 3D seismic acquisition and processing. The required seismic coverage is 250 sq km for Cerera, 250 sq km for Areca-Bruni, 500 sq km for South Tanimbar, and 200 sq km for Namori, the statement said. Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said on May 20 that the government was accelerating exploration and development to support a national oil production target of 900,000 to 1 million barrels per day by 2029. As of May 2026, the ministry had identified 118 prospective oil and gas working areas. Indonesia produced 605,300 b/d of crude oil in 2025 and is targeting 610,000 b/d in 2026. Indonesia, a former OPEC member, has been seeking to attract more investment in its oil and gas sector as production continues to decline. Despite plans to shift toward cleaner energy, the government said oil and gas will remain important in meeting the country's growing energy needs during the transition. — Anita Nugraha, Sambit Mohanty Europe, Middle East and Africa Benin rejoins ranks of oil exporters as first Seme cargo sails to Europe  Some 360,000 barrels heading to Rotterdam  Field shuttered in 1998 amid falling prices  Heavy sweet crude similar Niger's Meleck Benin has lifted its first cargo of domestically produced Seme crude, ending a 28-year production hiatus, with the first heavy sweet barrels heading to the Netherlands, according to ship- tracking data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea. Exports to China reached 1.571 million b/d, up 20% month on month and up 42.9% year on year, CAS data showed. Futures had come under pressure from a broader de- escalation narrative in crude, fed by recent comments from President Donald Trump suggesting further military escalation may not be necessary, and by talk of a possible deal between the US and Iran, said Razan Hilal, a StoneX market analyst. “The tension for traders is that strikes on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz continue even as the charts turn lower,” she said. January cargoes could be priced below December barrels, which were concluded at premiums of $23-$25/b to ICE Brent futures on a DES Shandong basis, the sources said. Commercial crude stocks climbed 4.66 million barrels to 414.42 million barrels during the period, EIA data showed. The build was the largest since the week ended Aug. 7 and narrowed the deficit to the EIA’s seasonal five-year average to 4.3% from 5.2% the week prior. Crude stocks climbed across all regions, but the build was concentrated on the US Gulf Coast, where stocks moved 3.3 million barrels higher to 230.49 million barrels. Inventories at the NYMEX delivery hub of Cushing, Oklahoma, climbed 110,000 barrels to 27.36 million barrels, a three-week high and 9.5% above average for this time of year. SPR stocks declined 2.65 million barrels to 279.54 million barrels and were the lowest since October 1982. The draw was the largest since late August and marked a significant acceleration in weekly declines, which had averaged at around 200,000 barrels during October. Total net crude averaged at 3.24 million barrels per day during the period, up 20% from the week prior and the highest since the week ended Sept. 4. Exports slowed 6% to a three-week low of 3.46 million b/d while imports were up 5.1% at 6.7 million b/d. All rights reserved. 2 Asia Pacific Thin refining buffers expose jet fuel to fresh price spikes in 2027  Low inventories heighten supply risks  Diesel demand squeezes jet fuel output  Asian refining shift lengthens trade routes Jet fuel markets face renewed price spikes in 2027 as depleted inventories and limited spare refining capacity leave supply vulnerable to disruptions, panelists said at the IATA Aviation Energy Forum in Guangzhou Nov. 11. While there were reasons for near-term optimism, the market could tighten again next year without an easing of disruptions involving the Middle East and Russia, said Rob McLeod, global head of commodity risk solutions at Hartree Partners. “We’ve drawn down to exceptionally low inventory levels,” McLeod said. “Absent those possibilities, we’ve got these huge risks with very little buffer.” A US Gulf Coast hurricane, for example, could expose the lack of a refining buffer and trigger renewed price spikes, he said. “There’s a lot of cause for concern about potential spikes next year.” The warning comes after global jet fuel stocks continued edging lower in October as demand outstripped supply, with refiners focused on maximizing diesel yields, according to S&P Global Energy CERA's November outlook. The global jet fuel crack averaged $72/b in September and is forecast to strengthen to $74/b in the fourth quarter, then ease to $51/b in the first quarter of 2027 and $40/b in the second quarter. That expected easing nevertheless comes as underlying aviation demand strengthens. CERA sees global jet fuel demand rebounding by 1.17 million b/d in 2027, following a 255,000 b/d decline in 2026. James Simpson, global head of aviation research at S&P Global Energy, also warned that jet fuel markets would remain exposed to volatility. “I don’t think the world is going to ease into a calmer place next year,” Simpson said. Refining availability has become a more important constraint on jet fuel supply than crude production, McLeod said, with crude supply comparatively more comfortable than refining availability this year. “Nowadays really refining is the key constraint,” he said. Diesel competition Jet fuel's outlook remains closely tied to diesel, with shortages in the larger middle distillate market feeding into aviation fuel availability and pricing, Simpson said. “The diesel’s tightness is going to continue to drive jet tightness,” he said. S&P Global Energy's November outlook put diesel markets as “very tight,” amid sharply reduced Middle Eastern exports and a prolonged Russian diesel export ban. The tightness has encouraged refiners to optimize diesel yields even as jet fuel inventories and exports decline. In Asia, that competition is particularly visible ahead of winter. Singapore jet/kerosene cracks against Dubai strengthened $10.4/b to $66.2/b, while the jet-diesel regrade discount widened to $8.3/b in October, according to CERA’s Asia outlook. Asian cracks are expected to remain elevated in November and December amid winter heating oil demand and tight middle distillates markets. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the FOB Singapore jet fuel/kerosene crack against Dubai crude at $59.55/b Nov. 11. Over the longer term, electrification could reduce gasoline demand and encourage refinery closures even as aviation fuel consumption continues to grow, Simpson said. Diesel consumption from trucking, mining and agriculture is also likely to prove more resilient than gasoline demand. “If you’re knocking out demand for gasoline down the line, you’re going to have less refining,” he said. That would leave a smaller refining base facing competing requirements for middle distillates, increasing pressure on refiners to choose which products to produce, he added. The lack of spare capacity also limits the industry's ability to replace lost production during outages, Simpson noted. However, proximity to refining capacity alone does not guarantee secure supply, McLeod said. Outages and export restrictions can still disrupt availability, making diversification of supply sources important. Longer supply chains The shift in refining capacity toward Asia and the Middle East is also increasing importing regions' exposure to longer supply chains, freight costs and geopolitical disruptions, the speakers said. Simpson cited jet fuel shipments from South Korea to Europe as an example of the distances required to meet European demand. McLeod said the spread between Northwest European and Singapore jet fuel benchmarks had widened in recent months, reflecting higher freight costs and Europe's import dependence. ©2026 S&P Global Inc. For Australian carriers purchasing fuel priced against Singapore benchmarks, the freight component also creates exposure that must be managed, whether borne directly by the airline or incorporated into a supplier's premium, he said. Simpson cautioned that freight increases were smaller than swings in jet fuel cracks, although the two costs compounded the burden for import-dependent buyers. Energy-security concerns could temper the pace of European refinery closures, Simpson said, while McLeod pointed to both strong refining profitability and the possibility of policy support. Still, retaining local capacity would not eliminate disruption risks, the speakers said, with diversified sources and spare refining capacity offering additional protection. — Mia Pei South Korea extends auto fuel tax cuts, retains MOPS-linked price caps  Seoul retains 15% gasoline, 25% diesel tax cuts  More than 90% of Nov-Dec crude requirements secured  Price cap policy to reference Platts MOPS benchmarks South Korea will extend auto fuel tax cuts for two months through Jan. 31, 2027, as refiners remain vigilant about securing crude supplies amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, the finance and trade ministries said Nov. 11. The extension comes after the country secured close to 100% of its monthly crude requirements so far during the second half of 2026, while the government and refining industry continue to monitor potential supply disruptions, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said in a statement. The decision was made at a meeting of economy-related ministers to account for “the need to ease the burden on households ahead of the winter season and the government’s capacity to respond to future price volatility,” the Ministry of Finance and Economy said in a policy briefing report. The government will remain vigilant and maintain an emergency response system to ensure stable energy supplies and prices, according to the finance and trade ministries. The current tax cuts of 15% on gasoline and 25% on diesel and butane will remain in place through Jan. 31, 2027, the finance ministry said. The cuts had been scheduled to expire Nov. 30. The trade ministry said South Korea had secured more than 90% of the crude oil volumes imported in November and December of the previous year, along with more than 90% of expected December naphtha requirements, limiting concerns about near-term refinery feedstock shortfalls. MOPS-based price-cap policy At the Nov. 11 meeting, the government decided to retain the fuel price-cap scheme introduced March 13, under which it sets maximum prices for gasoline, diesel and kerosene to prevent sharp increases in retail fuel prices. The price ceilings are calculated using average supply prices for regular gasoline, diesel and kerosene, with adjustments linked to the Mean of Platts Singapore, or MOPS, benchmark and related taxes, according to the trade ministry. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the outright 92 RON gasoline MOPS strip at an average of $108.66/barrel so far in November, down from the October average of $139.48/b but higher than the 2025 average of $78.81/b. The Asian gasoline outright benchmark was last assessed at $102.05/b on Nov. 11. Platts assessed the outright 10 parts per million gasoil MOPS at $150.94/b on Nov. 11, compared with the October average of $173.02/b and the 2025 average of $87.73/b. Retail auto fuel prices have remained relatively stable, supported by the tax cuts and price-cap scheme, the trade ministry said. Diesel pump prices averaged 1,842 won/liter ($1.38/liter) in the first week of November, down from 2,005 won/liter six months earlier, according to data from state-run Korea National Oil Corp. Gasoline pump prices averaged 1,855 won/liter over the same period, down from 2,011 won/liter six months earlier, KNOC data showed. Domestic demand, exports The measures come as South Korean demand for refined oil products fell 13.1% year over year in September, marking the eighth consecutive monthly decline amid weaker consumption of diesel, jet fuel and naphtha, according to KNOC data. ©2026 S&P Global Inc. The government relaxed restrictions on diesel exports effective Nov. 1 in response to requests from domestic refiners seeking greater flexibility to capitalize on robust international middle distillate cracks and export margins. Under the revised measure, refiners may export up to 110% of year-earlier diesel volumes for the same month, up from the previous ceiling of 100%. The government introduced restrictions on gasoline, diesel and kerosene exports March 13 amid concerns over supply disruptions following the start of the war in the Middle East and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. — Gawoon Philip Vahn and Charles Lee Europe, Middle East and Africa COP31: Saudi minister warns climate push risks failure without energy security  Minister advocates balancing climate with economy, security  COP31 targets 35% electricity in global energy consumption  Renewables reach 15.6% of Saudi grid capacity Saudi Arabia is approaching climate action through “multiple pathways”, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Nov. 11, while warning that pursuing carbon neutrality without securing energy supplies risks undermining global climate efforts. “Successful climate action cannot be achieved by imposing a single pathway, but rather by delivering shared outcomes through multiple pathways that protect the climate, support countries' development and respect their individual circumstances,” Bin Salman said in a speech at the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey. Saudi Arabia's approach “combines cutting emissions on the one hand and energy security and sustainable development on the other hand,” Bin Salman said. Electrification debate Bin Salman's remarks came as electrification emerged as the defining theme of COP31. The centerpiece of the summit's agenda is the Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to raise electricity's share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035. However, meeting that target would require accelerating the pace of electrification by approximately fourfold, as well as significantly increased investment in electrified technologies. Bin Salman offered a measured take on the pledge. “The expansion of electrification does not necessarily lead to lower emissions unless the sources of its production are taken into account, and countries are given the flexibility to choose pathways that suit their circumstances and priorities, while maintaining energy security and supporting economic development,” he said. Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude oil exporter, is also facing dual chokepoint pressures as maritime trade through the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz faces disruption, forcing a diversification of shipping routes to maintain global oil supply flows. “The current geopolitical developments have affirmed what the kingdom has warned against for many years,” Bin Salman said. “The quest for carbon neutrality without guaranteeing energy security can undermine our efforts.” He also pushed back against climate measures that could constrain economic development. “The measures that are aimed at protecting the climate should not constitute barriers facing countries and impeding their achievements of economic development,” Bin Salman said. Domestic transition Despite its status as a top crude oil exporter, Saudi Arabia has positioned itself as an active participant in the clean energy transition. It has committed to a 2060 net-zero target and is investing heavily in renewables, hydrogen and nuclear power. Nearly a third of the country's renewable energy program has been completed and connected to the grid, while the kingdom has made 15% to 20% progress in displacing 1 million b/d of crude oil from its power mix, Mohammed al-Ibrahim, assistant energy minister for oil and gas, said at the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh on Oct. 14. Renewables accounted for 15.6% of total electricity generation capacity by the end of 2025, according to the Saudi Ministry of Energy. Total electricity consumption across residential, commercial, industrial and other sectors reached 358 terawatt-hours in 2025, according to data published by the Saudi Ministry of Economy and Planning on Oct. 11. — Lulwa Albuainain, Eklavya Gupte ©2026 S&P Global Inc. All rights reserved. 5 UK expands sanctions on Russian oil production, shadow fleet  Includes Rosneft’s Vostok Oil  Targets vessels supplying Russian oil, LNG The UK government said Nov. 12 that it has sanctioned more Russian oil production as well as shadow fleet vessels involved in supplying Russian oil and LNG, as it targets nearly every part of the energy revenue chain. The new listings include Slavneft, which holds licenses for oil and gas exploration and production across 35 blocks in west and east Siberia, according to the company’s website. Most of its production is carried out in the Khanty-Mansi region. It also owns the Yanos and Mozyr refineries. This makes the UK the first country to have sanctioned all of Russia’s top 10 oil producers, the government said in a statement. The UK has also sanctioned Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project. Launched in September, most production from the project’s key fields, Vankor and Payakha, is shipped via the Northern Sea Route, which runs through Russia’s Arctic waters. Supplies from the project averaged 89,000 barrels/day in September and 24,000 b/d in October, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea. Deliveries will face challenges in the winter when the open-water navigation window closes and tankers require icebreaker escort. Rosneft said previously that Vostok Oil could supply up to 30 million metric tons of oil as early as the second half of 2027, rising to 50 million mt by 2030, subject to market demand and favorable economic conditions. The UK announced the new sanctions as Prime Minister Andy Burnham said peace talks on Ukraine have progressed, but pressure must be ramped up on Russia to agree a full and immediate ceasefire. Negotiators have so far failed to reach a deal to end the full- scale invasion of Ukraine, which began in February 2022. Future talks are expected to include energy, which has been a major target for both sides in recent months. Ukraine is bombarding Russia’s refining network, and Russia is striking Ukrainian power infrastructure. — Rosemary Griffin US producer Murphy Oil inks contracts for four blocks off Cameroon  Licenses cover total of 2.6 million acres  Murphy dominated nation's last bid round  Cameroon aims to for 100,000 b/d output Houston-based Murphy Oil has signed production sharing contracts for four oil blocks off Cameroon, the company said in a statement Nov. 11, as the Central African country looks to revive its struggling upstream sector. In a release on its website, Murphy said the PSCs concern the Elombo, Etinde Exploration, Ntem and Tilapia exploration licenses, covering a total of 2.6 million acres. “Murphy, through its subsidiary, will initially hold a 100 percent working interest and serve as operator,” the company said, adding that state-run Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures “retains the right to participate in any future development with up to a 20 percent working interest.” “Murphy and SNH will now work together to further evaluate the exploration potential of the four blocks,” the statement added. The deals follow Cameroon’s last oil and gas licensing round, which wound up in March and was dominated by Murphy, according to Cameroonian officials. It comes on the heels of a busy few weeks for the US producer, which on Nov. 3 said it had signed a pair of production sharing contracts with Mauritania for the C10 and Tiof offshore blocks. Murphy, which has assets in the US, Canada, Vietnam and Cote d’Ivoire, pumped 182,294 barrels of oil equivalent/day of oil and gas in 2025. Its African operations are focused on Cote d’Ivoire, where it recently made a commercial discovery with its Bubale-1X exploration well. New bid round Cameroon last month launched a new six-block licensing round, in a bid to double its oil output from the current 50,000 barrels/day, according to SNH. The African country has underperformed its peers in recent years, with a wave of new exploration activity currently occurring along Africa’s Atlantic coastline. It boasts 200 million barrels of proven oil reserves, according to the US Energy Information Administration, and produced 186,000 b/d at its peak in 1985, but has seen underinvestment, field maturation and IOC exits, including by US supermajor ExxonMobil, dent production. Cameroon’s medium sweet Kole crude grade finds buyers in China and Asia, while the country is also the sole export route for some 130,000 b/d of Chadian crude through a cross-border pipeline. — Charlie Mitchell ©2026 S&P Global Inc. All rights reserved. 6 Orlen still sees Qatar as ‘important’ LNG supplier after SPA termination  Says it has secured ‘more attractive’ terms than oil- indexed deal  Replacing missing volumes mainly with US cargoes  Poland YOY LNG imports down YTD, US share up: CERA Poland’s Orlen continues to see QatarEnergy as a key LNG supplier, even after canceling one of two long-term LNG sale and purchase agreements with the major producer earlier this week amid its months-long force majeure due to the war in the Middle East, the company told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, on Nov. 12. “QatarEnergy remains an important LNG supplier to Orlen,” a spokesperson said. The spokesperson explained that the terminated contract — an oil-indexed agreement signed in 2009 — was less favorable than other existing options. “We have secured more attractive gas purchase and supply terms than those available under that agreement,” the spokesperson said. “We are replacing the missing volumes primarily with supplies from the United States. We also source gas from Norway, including from our own production, delivered through Baltic Pipe.” The comments affirm recent assessments from market watchers, who highlighted the cost of the oil-linked deal as a probable motivation for terminating the 2009 QatarEnergy agreement when possible. Analysts warned that other offtakers with similar pricing terms could likewise terminate deals with Doha should the force majeure persist and their contracts allow it. The other QatarEnergy deal that Orlen has maintained is priced on a natural gas basis. US volumes The Orlen spokesperson stressed that cargoes from Venture Global’s Plaquemines LNG export terminal in Louisiana have bolstered its portfolio “since November.” Venture Global said late last month that it had begun commercial operations at the first phase of the project, almost two years after the terminal began exporting cargoes. Orlen has a 20-year offtake commitment for 4 million metric tons/year from Plaquemines. Poland has brought in about 4.8 million mt of LNG so far this year, with volumes from the US accounting for some 89% of imports, according to data from S&P Global Energy CERA. Across the same span in 2025, it imported roughly 5.3 million mt of the super-chilled fuel, with US volumes only accounting for 73% of cargoes, per CERA. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the DES Northwest Europe LNG marker at $27.585/million British thermal units on Nov. 11, up 1% day over day. — Matt Hoisch UAE's Ras al-Khaimah airport jet demand may more than double in five years: CEO  Passenger traffic projected to double by 2032  ADNOC holds exclusive fuel supply concession The Ras al-Khaimah International Airport in the UAE’s northern emirate Ras al-Khaimah expects passenger traffic to almost double by 2032, leading jet fuel demand to more than double, CEO Manish Seth told Platts in an interview on Nov. 11. The airport serves 1.2 million to 1.3 million passengers a year, with the UAE’s state-run Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. as the exclusive provider of jet fuel under a concession that expires at the end of next year, Seth said, speaking on the sidelines of the Ras al-Khaimah Investment and Business Summit. “Our number of weekly flights or number of daily flights is going to almost double. reports.ftext: Volume 104 / Issue 218 / November 12, 2026 (continued on page 21) Market analysis International Crude Platts Dubai differential flips to discount amid poor Mid-East crude demand  Platts Dubai assessed at discount for first time since mid-July  Middle East crude supplies resilient despite Iranian attacks  Asian refiners make larger purchases of West African, Brazilian crudes Middle East crude benchmark Platts cash Dubai saw its differential against Dubai futures flip into discounts for the first time in almost four months on Nov. 12, amid ample regional supplies and signs that Asian refiners were switching to larger sweet crude purchases from the West. The marker was assessed down 44 cents/b day over day at a 12 cents/b discount to same-month Dubai futures at the Nov. 12 Asian close, data from Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, showed. It was last assessed at a discount of minus 30 cents/b to Dubai futures on July 17, the data showed. The Middle East crude complex had already started the January-loading trade cycle in November on a sharply weaker note, with the Platts Dubai differential having slipped at the start of the month similarly to lows not seen since mid-July, Platts data showed. At least three Singapore-based crude traders have reported poorer demand from Asian refiners for Middle East crudes this month, while a sizeable overhang of December-loading cargoes, as well as December-arrival Iraqi barrels, were heard to have been carried over into the new January-loading cycle. That weakness has lasted up to the present day. Chinese independent refiners, for one, have increasingly turned to more competitive alternatives from West Africa, Brazil and Iraq. Among recent trades heard, at least 5 million barrels of Brazilian crude grades including Sururu, Sepia and Tupi for December and January arrivals have been sold to at least three independent refiners at premiums in the $16-$20s/b range to ICE Brent crude futures on a delivered basis, according to several trade sources. West African crude traders have similarly reported firmer demand from Chinese independent refiners, with Angola’s Plutonio, Mostarda and Dalia, in addition to Ceiba from Equatorial Guinea and Djeno from the Republic of Congo for late November and December loading among the grades recently sold to the sector. (continued on page 3) OIL FUTURES: Crude climbs after Trump says US doesn’t need deal with Iran  Trump says no deal with Iran needed; market eyes tense status quo  Strait of Hormuz traffic drops to 15 ships  Saudi crude exports hit 7.5 million b/d as ex-Yanbu flows climb Crude oil futures settled higher Nov. 12 as hopes for a near- term US-Iran peace agreement faded after US President Donald Trump said he did not need a deal with Tehran. NYMEX December WTI settled $2.21/barrel higher at $88.74/b an ceICE January Brent climbed $3.06/b to end the session at $95.82/b. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump said in a Nov. 12 post to his social media platform Truth Social. NYMEX December RBOB settled 6.33 cents/gallon lower at $2.6708/gal and December ULSD climbed 7.52 cents/gal to $4.2865/gal. “Risk premium back on the menu,” TD Securities Analyst Ryan McKay and Bart Melek said in a Nov. 12 note. “The latest headlines from President Trump, that no deal with Iran is needed, have poured cold water on deal optimism.” Vessel transits via the Strait of Hormuz remain constrained amid persistent attacks on shipping; however, the advent of robust alternative routes has led to Middle East crude flows stabilizing at near pre-war levels. Indian refiners have also picked up Brazilian crudes as well as sizeable volumes of Iraqi barrels over several buy tenders since mid-October, according to trade sources and Platts compilation of trade data. These come against a backdrop of ample Middle East crude flows and offers that have remained relatively resilient despite ongoing Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz. S&P Global Commodities at Sea data showed crude oil exports directly exiting the Persian Gulf through the Strait held below 5 million barrels/day for most of October, ending the month at 4.4 million b/d. One Singapore-based trader had noted in the prior week ended Nov. 6 that Iraqi crude production was back to pre-war levels, while adding that ample offers were still being floated in the market for December-arrival Basrah crudes. “There are still a lot of offers for this product. Everything is loading,” the trader said. — Yong ren Toh, Alvinn Philips, Daisy Xu - Oil Market Specialist, George Delaney Chinese independent refiners eye cheaper crude alternatives, pressuring ESPO prices  Jan ESPO price could fall  Dec ESPO barrels at ICE Brent plus $23-$25/b  Iraqi Basrah trades at $7-$9/b premium Russian ESPO crude prices could weaken for January-delivery cargoes as Chinese independent refiners increasingly turn to more competitive alternatives from West Africa, Brazil and Iraq, refinery and trade sources told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, on Nov. 12. China's independent refiners are the main buyers of the Far East-loading ESPO barrels, taking about 3.1 million metric tons of the 4.1 million mt loaded in October, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea data and trade sources. January cargoes could be priced below December barrels, which were concluded at premiums of $23-$25/b to ICE Brent futures on a DES Shandong basis, the sources said. The sources attributed the high premiums for December cargoes to tighter supply. Market availability may fall by three to four cargoes, equivalent to about 300,000-400,000 mt, according to a source at an independent refinery in Shandong. While tighter supply supported December premiums, refiners expected demand to drive the market for January cargoes. West African crude Dalia for January delivery was sold at premiums of about $10.7/b to ICE Brent futures on a DES Shandong basis on Nov. 12, while Djeno was priced at premiums of about $9/b on the same basis, drawing greater interest from Chinese independent refiners, trade sources said. A Shandong-based trader also expected ESPO premiums to face downward pressure as lower freight costs made West African barrels more competitive, although tighter supply could keep January ESPO prices around current levels. The widening price gap has given Chinese independent refiners greater flexibility to optimize their crude slates, with some buyers that previously relied on Iranian crude increasingly turning to Iraqi Basrah grades. “For independent refineries, they can buy West African crudes if they are cheaper and Basrah Medium if Iranian crude becomes less available,” the trader said. Sweet barrels draw interest Chinese independent refiners switching from Iranian crude to Basrah Medium still need sweeter barrels from West Africa or Brazil to balance the higher sulfur content of their crude slates, refinery and trade sources said. A Dongying-based independent refiner bought 3 million barrels of Tupi crude for January arrival at a premium of about $18/b over March ICE Brent futures on a DES Shandong basis. The deal put the Brazilian grade below recent ESPO levels and highlighted the availability of competitively priced alternative sweet crude as Chinese independent refiners reduced their intake of Russian barrels. Chinese independent refiners imported a combined 4.4 million mt of Russian crude in October, down 18.5% from September, according to data collected by Platts from refinery and trade sources. Of the October total, about 3.1 million mt was ESPO crude, down from 3.4 million mt in September, the data showed. Private mega-refiners imported about 10 ESPO cargoes in October and remained among the biggest buyers of the grade, according to the data. Basrah barrels add to competition Ample supplies of Iraqi Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy for December delivery were competing with ESPO, particularly among refiners seeking alternatives to Iranian crude. Basrah Heavy for December delivery was reported to have concluded at a premium of about $7/b to ICE Brent futures, while Basrah Medium traded at about $9/b on the same basis, according to trade sources. “That is almost the cheapest crude available to independent refineries for the time being,” a Shandong-based trader said. The trader said Basrah offers could edge lower from current levels as geopolitical tensions eased. — Daisy Xu - Oil Market Specialist, Oceana Zhou - Oil Market Specialist Kuwait Petroleum cuts Asia-bound Dec. crude OSP differential by $2/b  Asia-bound Dec. This included delivery of 4.576 million mt to Atyrau, 4.762 million mt to PetroKazakhstan, 5.424 million mt to Pavlodar and 760,000 b/d to Caspi Bitum, KazTransOil said. — Rosemary Griffin CPC Blend differential rebounds despite oversupplied environment  Weak base level attracts buying interest  Ample supply limits upside Differentials for CPC Blend cargoes were heard to be strengthening on Nov. 12 despite abundant supply in the Mediterranean sweet crude market. Two crude traders in the region noted that first-decade December CPC Blend loaders have largely been placed. The cargoes were heard to have changed hands at discounts of between $4.50/b to $4/b to Dated Brent, marking an improvement from last reported levels. “The freight has dropped a lot the last couple of weeks. That has helped arb a few cargoes [to Northwest Europe],” said one trader, but noted that the Mediterranean basin remained the primary outlet for the grade. While the regional sweet crude complex remained “under pressure,” CPC Blend cargoes have been supported from their low base. Supply fundamentals within the Mediterranean sweet crude basin remained largely unchanged over the past week. However, the softening freight environment catalyzed a rebound in differentials and sparked interest in the grade. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the dirty Black Sea-Mediterranean Suezmax freight route at 440w Nov. 12, down from 970w on Oct. 30. “CPC [Blend] is not struggling for now. It's the cheapest grade, so feels like the demand is there... for now,” the second trader said. The uptick in activity also followed the release of the December loading program for the flagship Kazakh grade earlier in the week. Kazakh-origin CPC Blend crude loadings are set to average between 1.4 million-1.5 million barrels/day in December, according to data collated by Mediterranean crude traders with direct knowledge of loading schedules. At current levels, CPC Blend volumes may not have to rely heavily on arbitrage options beyond the Mediterranean, the second trader added. While arbitrage economics of moving volumes to the NWE were open, flows to Asia remain stifled by long-haul freight, backwardation, and competitively priced Murban in the East-of- Suez market. Platts assessed CPC Blend CIF Augusta Suezmax cargoes at a discount of $6.10/b to Dated Brent, up $1.50/b on the day. — Ernest Puey JAPAN DATA: Refinery product prices rise 16% YOY in Oct  BOJ reports seventh straight monthly increase  Gasoline prices decline 2.53% from year ago  Import costs surge 66%, led by jet fuel Japan's petroleum refinery product prices in the producer price index rose 15.52% year over year in October, marking the seventh consecutive monthly increase, the Bank of Japan said Nov. 12. The PPI “covers domestically produced and domestically traded goods in the corporate sector,” the BOJ said. According to the BOJ, gasoline prices in the PPI fell 2.53% year over year in October, the fourth consecutive monthly decline. Meanwhile, all price indexes for jet fuel oil, kerosene, gasoil, A-fuel oil and B/C-fuel oil rose year over year in October. Prices of petroleum refinery products in the yen-based import price index rose 66.26% year over year in October, the eighth consecutive monthly increase, the BOJ said. Gasoline, jet fuel oil, kerosene and B/C-fuel oil prices rose 81.48%, 106.94%, 105.96% and 90.46%, respectively, from a year earlier, all accelerating from September. All rights reserved. 2 ERIA outlines 90-day ASEAN oil-stockpiling framework, urges pilots with existing infrastructure  ERIA proposes 450 million barrel regional reserve  Ticketing system enables shared stock usage ASEAN should pursue voluntary oil-stockpiling arrangements that combine national reserves, contractual emergency-access rights, and joint stocks, the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia said Nov. 12, outlining a framework modeled on 90 days of regional oil demand. The proposals envisage total coverage of about 450 million barrels, comprising an assumed 150 million barrels of eligible existing refinery and commercial inventories (30-day coverage) and 300 million barrels of additional strategic stocks (60-day strategic reserve layer). It comes as Nikkei reported Nov. 12 that a scheme led by ERIA could begin as early as 2027, initially allowing the Philippines to buy gasoline and diesel stored in Indonesia and Thailand during emergencies. ERIA is a Jakarta-headquartered think tank led by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. ERIA recommends starting with small public-private pilots among interested countries, rather than immediately establishing a single ASEAN-wide reserve. “Progress need not wait until every element of a comprehensive regional system is in place,” wrote ERIA President Tetsuya Watanabe. Emergency access, not common ownership The proposal includes a ticketing system that provides contractual access to stocks held by another party in return for a fee, without requiring the buyer to construct dedicated storage or purchase the inventory upfront. Commodity settlement at drawdown would remain a separate obligation where applicable, according to ERIA. Joint stockpiling could involve producer- or supplier-owned oil stored in ASEAN facilities, with participating countries securing emergency access rights and contributing to storage and related costs. ERIA also outlines a deeper cooperation model involving shared investment, access rights and potentially ownership of reserve capacity. Under the study’s most cooperative scenario, the additional 60-day strategic layer is split into 25 days of national stocks, five days of ticketed stocks and 30 days of joint stocks. At the assumed regional demand of 5 million b/d, these represent 125 million, 25 million, and 150 million barrels, respectively. Regarding the 150 million barrels of assumed 30-day contribution from refineries and commercial inventories, ERIA cautioned against automatically counting them as emergency reserves, noting that their emergency availability still needs to be verified. Building on APSA The proposed arrangements would complement the ASEAN Framework Agreement on Petroleum Security and its coordinated emergency-response measures, rather than create a parallel regional institution, ERIA said. Six of ASEAN’s 11 members had ratified APSA as of end- October, the ASEAN Center for Energy told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. ACE Executive Director Razib Dawood previously said the target was to complete ratification before the November ASEAN summit. ERIA said that the renewed APSA, once in force, would provide a regional framework for petroleum security cooperation. Stockpiling pilots would help establish the commercial and operational arrangements needed to make emergency access workable. Testing delivery ERIA recommends testing the complete supply chain, from an emergency request and stock verification through release authorization, commercial settlement, loading, cross-border delivery and replenishment. “The supply emergency that triggers activation of the arrangement should not constitute a force majeure event,” the strategy said, distinguishing the crisis the arrangement is designed to address from separate events that make particular stocks inaccessible or delivery impracticable. The infrastructure assessment identifies 18 installations across 14 areas for further consideration, including Singapore’s Pulau Bukom and Jurong, Malaysia’s Pengerang, and Indonesia’s Dumai and Balongan. Repairs and reverse-flow pumping equipment to receive crude from vessels would be needed, ERIA said. The proposal also emphasizes that countries with limited refining capacity may need direct access to finished products rather than crude reserves. Greater cooperation could lower financing costs. ERIA estimates annualized stockholding costs of $2.19 billion under its most cooperative scenario, compared with $2.80 billion under the national-led portfolio, a saving of about $610 million, or 22%, at the same modeled reserve volume. However, equal nominal stock levels do not guarantee equivalent energy security, ERIA cautioned. Lower-cost arrangements would still need to demonstrate enforceable access rights, product compatibility, and reliable delivery during a disruption. — Mia Pei ©2026 S&P Global Inc. All rights reserved. 3 COSCO Energy prioritizes fleet renewal with 40 incoming VLCCs  Company secures 40 VLCCs via orders, charters  Deliveries target 2029-2030 replacement cycle  437 VLCCs expected over 20 years old by 2030 COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation is prioritizing replacement of aging vessels in its 40-VLCC newbuild program, with deliveries in 2029-2030 intended to maintain competitive capacity as its existing fleet ages, company executives said at a Nov. 12 third-quarter results briefing. The program comprises 10 directly ordered vessels and 30 to be taken on bareboat charter. Fleet renewal is the core objective, supplemented by moderate expansion, board secretary Ni Yidan said. “The average age of the company’s VLCC fleet continues to rise, and deliveries of the additional capacity are concentrated in 2029–2030, aligning with the existing fleet’s natural replacement cycle,” Ni said. Long shipbuilding lead times require the company to plan ahead to avoid a subsequent capacity gap, general manager Wang Mingfeng said. The comments elaborate on a program that includes 10 newbuild orders and 14 bareboat charters announced Nov. 9, alongside a separate 16-vessel leasing project involving COSCO Shipping Development. Ni said directly commissioning vessels would secure long-term capacity while allowing the company to influence ship design, energy-efficiency targets and technical standards. Secondhand vessel valuations are elevated, and ship condition varies, while short-term time charters are costly and capacity available for long-term charter commitments is relatively scarce, Ni said. The company secured relatively favorable prices and delivery schedules after market inquiries and competitive negotiations, Ni added. Bareboat charters would spread funding requirements and reduce the need for large upfront purchase payments, while bank loans and other financing instruments would also support the program, executives said. The company did not quantify how many of its existing VLCCs would be replaced or the net fleet growth expected from the 40-vessel program. The Platts Dirty Tanker Basis Global Index VLCC (Scrubber- Fitted Eco) dropped $44,862/day over the day to $821,189/day on Nov. 12. It was down from a record high of $1,195,157/day on Oct. 9, but above Feb. 27's $218,080/day. Delivery wave COSCO acknowledged that a concentration of industry newbuild deliveries in 2028–2029 could create temporary supply pressure, but said aging vessels and constraints on effective capacity would cushion the impact. The VLCC orderbook currently represents about 33% of the fleet, with deliveries concentrated in 2028 and 2029, Ni said. By 2030, 437 VLCCs are expected to be more than 20 years old, according to the company. Older vessels face declining competitiveness in operating efficiency, fuel consumption, maintenance, regulatory compliance, and charterer acceptance, Ni said. “Some new vessels will primarily replace existing tonnage, and net capacity additions are expected to be far below nominal deliveries,” Ni said. Actual available capacity is also constrained by dry-docking, declining efficiency as vessels age, and compliance and navigational safety restrictions, Ni added. On the demand side, normal crude procurement, potential inventory replenishment, changing trade flows and longer-haul cargo movements could continue to support ton-mile demand, according to Ni. “Concentrated deliveries may bring temporary market volatility, but replacement of older vessels, effective capacity constraints and replenishment demand will continue to support freight rate levels,” Ni said. — Mia Pei SINGAPORE DATA: Middle distillate stocks hit four-week high of 8.83 mil barrel  Gasoil imports surge 122.7%  Jet fuel exports rise 63.6% Singapore's onshore commercial middle distillate stocks rose 9.9% week over week to a four-week high of 8.83 million barrels over Nov. 5-11 as imports of both gasoil and jet fuel surged, according to data from Enterprise Singapore released Nov. 12. Stocks were last higher in the week ended Oct. 14, when they reached 10.38 million barrels, historical data showed. The city-state remained a net exporter of gasoil in the week ended Nov. 11, despite an increase in imports and a decline in exports. Net exports fell 42% week over week to 114,674 mt, according to Enterprise Singapore data. Gasoil imports rose to 97,481 mt over Nov. 5-11 from 43,776 mt a week earlier. South Korea was the top supplier with 45,505 mt, followed by China with 35,402 mt and Malaysia with 16,572 mt. Meanwhile, gasoil exports fell 12.2% week over week to 241,518 mt, with the Netherlands receiving the largest volume at 101,360 mt. Outflows to Malaysia, the top recipient in the previous week, fell 68.9% to 16,096 mt. Exports to New Zealand declined 41.4% to 26,654 mt, while outflows to Australia dropped 72.8% to 7,608 mt, according to the data. Singapore also supplied 22,845 mt of gasoil to Reunion, 21,337 mt to Papua New Guinea and 11,654 mt to Cambodia. The remaining exports of 4,526 mt were sent to the Solomon Islands, the data showed. ©2026 S&P Global Inc. All rights reserved. 4 Jet fuel exports rise Singapore remained a net exporter of jet fuel/kerosene over Nov. 5-11, with exports rising to 57,413 mt from 10,288 mt a week earlier, according to Enterprise Singapore data. Imports increased during the week, albeit from a low base, reaching 56.18 mt. Net exports were 63.4% higher, at 57,357 mt. The Netherlands was the largest export destination with 18,202 mt, followed by Australia with 14,182 mt, New Zealand with 12,942 mt and Reunion with 12,084 mt. European jet fuel imports remained strong amid tighter supply in the Atlantic Basin as critical inland freight routes, such as the Rhine and Danube, were operationally constrained, while Middle East output was forecast to fall below 815,000 barrels/day in the fourth quarter, according to S&P Global Energy CERA's November aviation outlook. Asia, especially South Korea and India, is expected to remain a major supplier of jet fuel to Europe in the fourth quarter. In Asia Pacific, airlines carried 259.3 million international passengers during the first eight months of 2026, up 2.1% year over year, highlighting strong passenger travel demand that translated into firm jet fuel consumption despite elevated ticket prices. — Mei huey Ng, Jenson Ong Three ships hit in 48 hours as Hormuz attacks persist  Iran claims ship hit mine in strait zone  Hormuz traffic stable at 18 ships on Nov. 12  Bab al-Mandab traffic falls to 27 ships Three commercial vessels were struck or attacked in the Persian Gulf and waters off Oman within 48 hours, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations, as navigation for ships through the Strait of Hormuz remains under pressure. The attacks targeted the NCC Fajr, Fujairah Energy and Dominica Prosperity between Nov. 10-11, recent UKMTO reports showed. Just 18 ships transited on Nov. 12, according to the latest S&P Global Commodities At Sea data. Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker Fujairah Energy, a tanker travelling eastbound in the Persian Gulf, was struck by an unknown projectile on Nov. 10, according to a Nov. 12 time-lagged report from UKMTO. India's Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways confirmed that four of the vessel's 22 crew were injured. The remaining 18 crew were reported safe. A day later, Omani authorities reported the Saudi Arabia-flagged chemicals/products tanker NCC Fajr came under attack north of Khasab, Oman at approximately 0200 UTC, with crew reported safe and environmental damage unknown, UKMTO said. The third vessel, the Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker Dominica Prosperity, was struck by an unknown projectile in its engine room on Nov. 11, 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras al Khaimah, UAE. Vanguard Tech reported that all 22 crew members, including 19 Indian nationals, were safely evacuated by the UAE Coast Guard with no injuries. Firefighting operations were ongoing at the time of the latest report. Mine warfare claims Iran's Revolutionary Guards said via state news channels on Nov. 13 that a liquefied gas carrier had struck a naval mine after ignoring warnings and traveling through what the IRGC described as an “unauthorized” route, adding that the vessel was escorted by US fighter jets. The claim follows a pattern of Iranian assertions that commercial vessels are striking mines along the US-backed transit corridor in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz that the Institute for the Study of War identified in a Nov. 12 update. Iran's mine claims were “likely to undermine ship operators' confidence in US escort operations and compel vessels to transit through Iranian territorial waters,” ISW said, adding it had “not observed any indicators that Iran has successfully re-mined the strait.” The Joint Maritime Information Center, in its Nov. 12 update, said “IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” adding that “these actions continue to demonstrate Iran's intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels.” Hormuz traffic on Nov. 12 comprised four VLCCs, one Aframax tanker, four product tankers, one LPG vessel, five bulk carriers, one container ship, one landing craft and one tug, with movements weighted toward outbound flows. Activity across the US naval blockade line rose to 65 transits from 59 the previous day, with 38 vessels entering the monitored zone, against 27 departures. According to Nov. 11 CENTCOM figures, nearly 150 commercial vessels have been redirected and five merchant ships disabled since the US enacted its maritime blockade in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM did not immediately respond to inquiries about US fighter jet escorts of ships in Hormuz. At Bab al-Mandab, traffic fell to 27 transits on Nov. 12 — the lowest level since Nov. 8 — with tanker activity split evenly between five vessels moving southbound and five heading northbound into the Red Sea. “Maritime risks in the region remained elevated,” the CAS report said. — Lauren Holtmeier Norway loses legal challenge against three offshore oil field permits  Court orders Oslo to re-examine permitting  Yggdrasil holds 800 mil barrels of resources  Production unaffected by court's ruling The Norwegian government has lost a legal challenge at the country’s Supreme Court brought by environmental groups against three prominent offshore oil fields, the court said in its ©2026 S&P Global Inc. Any unauthorized use of this copyrighted material constitutes infringement of our intellectual property and will subject you to possible legal action. Platts Oilgram News November 13, 2026 © 2026 by S&P Global Inc. All rights reserved. 5 decision released Nov. 13, although the case is not expected to impact hydrocarbon production. The lawsuit, filed by Greenpeace and Young Friends of the Earth, argued Oslo failed to assess the climate impact of so-called Scope 3 emissions — relating to the eventual burning overseas of the fields’ oil and gas — when it issued development permits for the projects. The suit concerned Aker BP’s key Yggdrasil field — which is expected to come online next year — and its Tyrving development, as well as state-run Equinor’s Breidablikk field. The latter two projects are already in production. Yggdrasil contains some 800 million barrels of oil equivalent of recoverable resources, including the Omega Alfa find, one of the Norwegian Continental Shelf’s largest discoveries in years. Meanwhile, Tyrving is a 25-million-barrel satellite project connected to Aker BP’s Alvheim area, and the 200-million- barrel Breidablikk field came online in 2023 with expected peak production of 55,000-60,000 b/d, according to Equinor. In its decision, the court said that the Energy Ministry “must reassess the case, on the basis of correct procedural errors.” According to the Financial Times, Norwegian Energy Minister Terje Aasland said the government would “correct the error in the permits that have been granted.” Crucially, the companies themselves were not parties to the case, meaning they are not required to suspend operations. Aker BP, Equinor and the Norwegian Energy Ministry did not respond to requests for comment from Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. Nevertheless, Haldis Tjeldflaat Helle, head of Greenpeace Norway, said in a statement that the “historic ruling will change Norwegian oil policy forever.” Natural declines Norwegian producers have been working hard to offset natural declines on the NCS by reviving shuttered fields, making new discoveries and undertaking infrastructure-led exploration to extend field life. The Norwegian Offshore Directorate has warned that oil and gas production could start to dip after 2027 without major new investments and finds. Aker BP, Equinor and fellow producer Var Energi recently joined forces to explore for frontier standalone fields, including in the Norwegian Arctic, which has proven controversial amid opposition from climate groups and the European Union. — Charlie Mitchell Iraq's Basrah crude exports rebound as more ships navigate Hormuz  October exports surge 21% to 3 million b/d  China purchases jump to 480,900 b/d  UAE imports average 540,000 b/d recently Iraq’s crude exports from Basrah rebounded to 3 million barrels/day in October, according to port loading data obtained exclusively by Platts Nov. 13. The data, sourced from a Basrah maritime agency, showed a 21% increase in export volumes month over month as more ships navigate the contested Strait of Hormuz. Some 56 ships loaded at Basrah's berths and single point moorings in October, up from 46 ships in September. Volumes have not yet surpassed prewar export volumes, which reached 3.24 million b/d in February, but October’s exports from the southern Basrah terminals are the closest yet, the data showed. Buying by China also rebounded, with 480,900 b/d of crude flowing to the East Asian country in October, compared to 99,000 b/d in September. China bought 355,000 b/d of Basrah Medium, with the remaining volumes Basrah Heavy. Before the war, China was the biggest buyer of Iraqi crude, but as China's total imports climbed back to a seven-month high of 9.92 million b/d, the share of Iraqi crude bound for China also increased. Exports to the UAE also remained elevated in October, reaching 597,800 b/d of predominantly Basrah Medium crude. Before regional war broke out at the tail end of February, the UAE rarely imported cargoes of Iraqi crude, but buying picked up in June, and imports have averaged about 540,000 b/d in the last three months, the data showed. — Lauren Holtmeier, Faleh Al-Khayat Russia strikes Naftogaz oil, gas facility in Chernihiv  Northern production site sees 'extensive damage'  Market watchers expect tough winter for war-torn country  Ukraine gas storage filled to 15.1 Bcm: CERA Russia attacked a Naftogaz oil and natural gas site in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, the state-owned energy company said late Nov. 12. The production facility in the country’s north sustained “extensive damage,” it said. There was also damage to processing equipment, according to Naftogaz. “This is yet another deliberate Russian attack on energy infrastructure as winter approaches,” Naftogaz acting CEO Serhiy Fedorenko said in the statement. “Fortunately, no employees were injured.” The assault is the latest in Moscow’s persistent targeting of Ukraine’s energy system as temperatures drop and the war-torn country enters what many expect to be a difficult winter. Ukraine’s gas stocks stood around 15.1 billion cubic meters as of Nov. 11, according to data from S&P Global Energy CERA. The fill is above the country’s initial winter stocking target of 14.6 Bcm, which it hit in August. Even with the healthy storage levels, Ukraine has also been securing support for further winter gas purchases to weather the heating season. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the month-ahead Dutch TTF gas price at €92.705/megawatt-hour on Nov. 12. While the index has subsided from recent highs, it remains some 201% higher than the same time a year ago. — Matt Hoisch ©2026 S&P Global Inc.
